patient.name: Kwame Mensah
patient.setting: Emergency Department (brought by ambulance from a restaurant)
patient.complaint: Swollen lips, noisy breathing and dizziness 10 minutes after eating a satay dish
background: Known peanut allergy (hives as a child); no auto-injector carried

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with sudden airway, breathing or circulation compromise minutes after a food, drug (often IV antibiotic), sting or latex, usually with skin or mucosal signs; then complications such as biphasic reactions.

points: Kwame, 16: satay chicken, then **tingling lips** within minutes.
Noisy breathing in, wheeze out; feels faint.
Hives spreading across chest and arms.

steps.lead: A sudden allergic reaction plus **airway** (stridor), **breathing** (wheeze, SpO2 89%) and **circulation** (BP 82/44) compromise: Kwame has anaphylaxis.

visual.title: Kwame's systolic BP on arrival
visual.label: Kwame 82
visual.caption: Circulation is compromised: this is not simple urticaria.

steps.lead: **Peanuts** are Kwame's trigger; other classics are shellfish, penicillins (especially IV co-amoxiclav), insect stings and latex.
Lip and tongue swelling, **inspiratory stridor** with expiratory wheeze, hoarse voice and poor perfusion: the full picture.

steps.q: What separates Kwame's anaphylaxis from simple urticaria?
o: Hives on more than one body area
steps.r: Anaphylaxis is defined by **A, B or C compromise** in the context of a sudden allergic reaction. Skin signs alone are urticaria or angioedema.

Anaphylaxis

steps.lead: Kwame's biggest immediate danger is **airway obstruction**; as a **teenager** he is also at high risk of a **biphasic** reaction.

steps.text: Skin signs are absent in a minority of anaphylaxis cases. Sudden wheeze or collapse after an IV antibiotic is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?' with mast cell tryptase, or the trap of delaying adrenaline for a test: anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis.

steps.q: Kwame's SpO2 is 89% and BP 82/44. What should happen before any blood test?
steps.r: Anaphylaxis is a **clinical diagnosis**: treat first with **IM adrenaline**. Tests never delay treatment.

steps.lead: Nobody waits for a result: Kwame's diagnosis is made at the bedside from the trigger and his **ABC** findings.
Once he is stable, **mast cell tryptase** is sent to confirm the reaction biochemically (the notes give 4 to 12 hours post-reaction).

visual.title: Mast cell tryptase after the reaction
visual.caption: Rises after degranulation, stays raised for hours, then returns to baseline (which is why a later baseline sample is also taken).

steps.title: Kwame's bloods
steps.text: Raised tryptase confirms mast cell degranulation; the lactate reflects his period of shock.
Tryptase is **retrospective** confirmation. It helps the allergy clinic, but a normal result never overrides a clear clinical picture.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' with IM adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 ml of 1:1000) into the anterolateral thigh for adults and over 12s, age-based doses for children, repeat after 5 minutes, then IV adrenaline infusion for refractory anaphylaxis and two auto-injectors on discharge.

steps.title: Resuscitation Council UK approach
nodes: Recognise: sudden A, B or C problem after a trigger
Call for help; remove the trigger; lie flat (sit if breathing is hard)
ABCDE: high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus
No improvement after 5 minutes → repeat IM adrenaline
Still compromised after 2 doses → refractory: IV adrenaline infusion
steps.caption: Adrenaline first; antihistamines and steroids are not life-saving.

steps.q: Kwame is 16. What dose of IM adrenaline does he need?
steps.r: Over 12s and adults: **500 micrograms IM (0.5 ml of 1:1000)**. 1 mg IV is the cardiac arrest dose.

steps.lead: Kwame's satay is taken away, his ID and allergies checked, and **500 micrograms IM adrenaline** goes into his **anterolateral thigh**.

visual.title: IM adrenaline dose by age (1:1000)
visual.label: Kwame 16 → 500 mcg
visual.caption: Age sets the dose: over 12 years gets the adult 500 micrograms.

steps.lead: Kwame gets **high-flow oxygen** (SpO2 89%), an **IV fluid bolus** for BP 82/44 and, still wheezy at 5 minutes, a **second IM adrenaline** dose.

visual.title: Kwame's response
visual.caption: Little change after dose 1; recovery after dose 2 at 5 minutes plus fluids.

steps.lead: Kwame improved after 2 doses. Had he still been compromised, this would be **refractory anaphylaxis**: expert help and an **IV adrenaline infusion**.

steps.text: Chlorphenamine and hydrocortisone do **not** treat airway swelling or shock. They are supportive only and must never delay or replace IM adrenaline.

steps.lead: Kwame needed 2 doses and is a teenager, so he is **admitted for observation**, then discharged with **two auto-injectors**, training and an allergy clinic referral.
Kwame's care follows the **Resuscitation Council UK** anaphylaxis algorithm, step by step.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the hypersensitivity type, which mediator causes which sign, which adrenaline receptor reverses which problem, why the thigh, and why reactions can return hours later.

steps.lead: Peanut protein **cross-links IgE** already sitting on Kwame's mast cells, which **degranulate** within minutes.

steps.title: From peanut to shock
nodes: Peanut allergen cross-links mast cell IgE

steps.lead: Each of Kwame's signs maps to a mediator effect: **leaky vessels** (lips, BP), **smooth muscle** (wheeze), **mucosal oedema** (stridor).

steps.q: Which adrenaline receptor action most directly reverses Kwame's hypotension and swelling?
steps.r: **Alpha-1** vasoconstriction raises BP and reduces oedema. Beta-1 increases cardiac output; beta-2 bronchodilates and reduces mediator release.

steps.lead: **Alpha-1** lifts Kwame's BP, **beta-1** boosts his heart, **beta-2** opens his airways; the **vastus lateralis** absorbs the drug fastest.
Kwame may react again hours later as new inflammatory cells arrive (**biphasic**); his raised **tryptase** is the lasting fingerprint of degranulation.

glossary.Anaphylaxis: A severe, life-threatening systemic allergic reaction with airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
glossary.Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate allergic reaction in which allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine.
glossary.IgE: Immunoglobulin E, the antibody that sits on mast cells and triggers immediate allergic reactions.
glossary.Mast cell: Tissue immune cell that releases histamine and tryptase when IgE on its surface is cross-linked.
glossary.Basophil: Blood white cell that, like mast cells, carries IgE and releases histamine.
glossary.Degranulation: Release of stored mediators such as histamine and tryptase from mast cells and basophils.
glossary.Histamine: Mediator that causes vasodilation, leaky vessels, itch and bronchial constriction.
glossary.Leukotrienes: Lipid mediators from mast cells that cause prolonged bronchoconstriction and vascular leak.
glossary.Prostaglandins: Lipid mediators released in anaphylaxis that add to vasodilation and bronchospasm.
glossary.Mast cell tryptase: Enzyme released from mast cells; a raised level confirms anaphylaxis after the event.
glossary.Tryptase: Mast cell enzyme measured in blood to confirm anaphylaxis.
glossary.Stridor: High-pitched noise on breathing in caused by upper airway narrowing.
glossary.Wheeze: Whistling expiratory sound from narrowed lower airways (bronchospasm).
glossary.See-saw breathing: Inspiratory stridor with expiratory wheeze, from upper airway swelling plus bronchospasm.
glossary.Angioedema: Swelling of the deeper skin and mucosa, often lips, tongue and throat.
glossary.Bronchospasm: Tightening of the airway smooth muscle causing wheeze.
glossary.Biphasic reaction: A second wave of anaphylaxis hours (typically 4 to 6) after the first, without re-exposure.
glossary.Refractory anaphylaxis: Breathing or circulation problems that persist despite two doses of IM adrenaline.
glossary.Adrenaline: First-line drug for anaphylaxis; acts on alpha and beta receptors.
glossary.IM adrenaline: Adrenaline injected into muscle, the anterolateral thigh, as first-line anaphylaxis treatment.
glossary.1:1000: Adrenaline strength of 1 mg in 1 ml, used for IM injection.
glossary.Vastus lateralis: Muscle of the outer thigh, the site for IM adrenaline.
glossary.Anterolateral thigh: Front and outer side of the thigh; the recommended IM adrenaline site.
glossary.Alpha-1: Adrenoceptor causing vasoconstriction, which raises BP and reduces swelling.
glossary.Beta-1: Adrenoceptor in the heart that increases rate and force of contraction.
glossary.Beta-2: Adrenoceptor causing bronchodilation and reducing mediator release from mast cells.
glossary.Auto-injector: A spring-loaded pen that delivers a fixed IM dose of adrenaline, such as an EpiPen.
glossary.ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: the structured emergency assessment.
glossary.Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, a penicillin antibiotic that is a classic anaphylaxis trigger.
glossary.Chlorphenamine: A sedating H1 antihistamine; supportive only in anaphylaxis.
glossary.Hydrocortisone: An IV corticosteroid; not a first-line or life-saving treatment in anaphylaxis.
glossary.Distributive shock: Low blood pressure from widespread vasodilation, as in anaphylaxis and sepsis.
glossary.Resuscitation Council UK: UK body that publishes the anaphylaxis treatment algorithm.
glossary.Hereditary angioedema: Inherited C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causing swelling without hives; does not respond well to adrenaline.
glossary.Vasovagal syncope: A faint from a reflex drop in heart rate and BP, with pallor and no rash.
